Probing chess based World Models

Nov 2026·Code

1 Introduction

A world model represents the state of an environment and predicts how it will change in response to an action. I chose chess because I can reconstruct that state after every move and check whether the model has kept track of the pieces. Grandmasters of similar strength can look at that same position and still express their own styles through the moves they prefer, whether they choose to attack, defend, or play for control of the centre. I can train a probe to predict the contents of each square from a chess model’s internal activity, then reuse the same probe on models trained on data from specific grandmasters. This matters now because world models are usually pretrained once and then fine-tuned for specific tasks, so we need to know whether a probe built on the original model can still read its state after its behaviour changes.

Chess lets me reconstruct the exact position after every move. I used four grandmasters’ different move preferences to test whether a probe trained on the original model could still read the board after fine-tuning.

  • RQ1. When fine-tuning changes the world model’s policy, how accurately can the original probe still read the board?
  • RQ2. How similarly do the different world models represent the board position, and is there a way to map one representation to another?

2 Models and controls

I started with Karvonen’s 25-million-parameter chess model, pretrained on about 16 million Lichess games. I fine-tuned four copies, one on each grandmaster’s own moves. For Anatoly Karpov and Garry Kasparov, I used games played in person. For Magnus Carlsen and Andrew Tang, I used online bullet games with one minute per player. Within each pair, I matched the amount of move text used for training and chose checkpoints on validation games.

I fine-tuned four copies of Karvonen’s 25M-parameter chess model, pretrained on about 16 million Lichess games. Karpov and Kasparov played in person. Carlsen and Tang played one-minute bullet online. I matched training budgets within each pair and selected checkpoints on validation games.

The bullet specialists trained on about six times as many games. Policy KL measures the shift in next-character predictions from the base, in nats per target character.

Did the choice of player change the moves? I compared the base and all four specialists on the same 1,500 positions. Within each pair, specialists trained on different players chose different moves about 14% of the time, versus 3–6.5% for two runs trained on the same player. Stockfish helped distinguish a stronger move from a preference between similarly good ones.

On 1,500 neutral boards, the specialists within each pair chose different moves about 14% of the time, versus 3–6.5% for two runs on the same player. I used Stockfish to score move quality.

What was the probe reading? For each pair, I fitted a linear probe to the base model, froze it, and scored piece type and colour on occupied squares from move 16. On in-person validation games, the largest drop in error came between layers 5 and 6, from 53.6% to 12.0%. At layer 6, a nonlinear probe (MLP) reached 8.0%, while a linear probe on an untrained model missed 85%. When I assigned fixed random labels to squares based on the last two moves, both probes stayed near chance. Most of the board signal the probes recovered was already readable with a linear probe.

From move 16, I scored piece type and colour on occupied squares. On in-person validation games, linear-probe error fell from 53.6% at layer 5 to 12.0% at layer 6 (8.0% with an MLP). Error was 85% on an untrained model, and both probes stayed near chance on the random-label task.

To check that the test could detect a wrong board, I replaced the internal activity for 5% of validation positions with activity from another game at the same move number. Error rose by 3.5 percentage points in both pairs, well above my preset tolerance of one point.

Replacing 5% of validation activations with another game’s at the same move number raised error by 3.5 points, above my one-point tolerance.

3 What changed in the first experiment

RQ1. How accurately the frozen probe read the board after fine-tuning

Each specialist gave its own player’s held-out moves a higher average log probability than the other specialist in its pair. The advantage was +0.008 nats per move for Karpov, +0.014 for Kasparov, +0.033 for Carlsen and +0.038 for Tang. It also held in reserved head-to-head games and across all 35 pairings of training runs in each experiment, including changes of seed and training sample.

All four selected checkpoints stayed within my tolerance of one extra error per hundred occupied squares. The largest increase was Karpov’s, from 12.14% on the base to 13.00% on the copy (+0.86 percentage points, 95% interval +0.79 to +0.94).

On the 380 positions where only one move came within half a pawn of Stockfish’s best, the specialists scored similarly to the base, with slightly lower observed accuracy: 61.6–63.9% versus 64.2% (234–243 correct choices versus 244).

In one held-out game, Tang’s copy took a rook on E3 with its queen. The base took it with its rook and allowed mate in two.

Which differences look like playing style

I scored each player’s moves after move 15 in held-out games and used the specialists’ relative scores to identify who played. Game-level AUC was 0.76 for Carlsen–Tang and 0.63 for Karpov–Kasparov (0.50 is chance). Across eight habits, including checks, captures and trades, the differences between the copies correlated with the players’ differences relative to the base model (r = 0.85 for Carlsen–Tang and 0.66 for Karpov–Kasparov).

In one game, the Karpov copy preferred moving its king to G5 over taking a pawn. In another, the Kasparov copy preferred checking with its queen over pushing a pawn. Stockfish rated the alternatives within half a pawn in both positions. Small preferences also changed how games unfolded. Against the same base-model opponent from 600 shared starts, just 32% of eligible Karpov–Kasparov sequences and 29% of Carlsen–Tang sequences still matched after ten of the specialists’ own moves. RQ2. How closely the specialists’ board representations matched

On the same boards, each specialist’s layer-6 activity shifted by about 12% of its original length (median). Positions close together in the base tended to stay close in each copy (rank correlation ≈ 0.99). Across the four copies, 32–36% of the squared change lay in the directions carrying 90% of the probe’s squared weights, below the 39–40% expected for a random subspace of the same size.

I fitted a rotation from each specialist back to the base model using paired positions, then tested the frozen probe on separate games. For Karpov, the rotation cut the extra error on occupied squares from 0.86 to 0.29 percentage points. For Kasparov, it fell from 0.52 to 0.01.

A rotation fitted on separate games cut Karpov’s excess error from 0.86 to 0.29 points and Kasparov’s from 0.52 to 0.01.

The selected checkpoints caught the pairs at different stages of training. When I compared all four copies at the same policy shift (KL = 0.01), the frozen probe’s extra error was 0.39–0.52 percentage points on in-person positions and 0.17–0.26 on bullet positions. By KL ≈ 0.04, even a freshly fitted linear probe had lost about 0.6–0.9 points on the in-person Karpov and Kasparov runs. Those runs show a gradual loss of linear readability as the policy moves further from the base. Probe error across training checkpoints

I pushed the internal signal for a movable white piece toward “empty” on 400 positions per pair. At medium strength, probability assigned to that piece’s legal moves fell 18.5% for Karpov, 17.2% for Kasparov, 10.2% for Carlsen and 9.5% for Tang, close to the respective base-model drops of 18.7% and 10.3%. Random edits of the same size changed it by less than 1%. The board signal remained readable and continued to influence moves.

4 Testing the frozen probe across Elo levels

All four specialists learned from grandmasters, and the copies in each pair chose the same move on about 86% of boards. My hunch is that players of similar strength often see the same strong moves. Across a wider range of Elo ratings, I’d expect differences in playing style and blunder rates to show up more clearly in the moves the models choose.

All four specialists learned from grandmasters. A wider range of Elo ratings should produce larger differences in their moves and blunder rates.

With another week, I’d fine-tune copies of the same base model on games from low, intermediate and high rating bands at one time control. Pooling games within each band could give me roughly ten times as much training data per copy. I’d match the training budgets and compare the copies on the same 1,500 held-out boards. If their move choices diverge more, I’d test whether the original frozen probe still reads the board within one extra error per hundred occupied squares relative to the base model. A consistent increase beyond that limit would change my conclusion.

I would match training budgets across low, intermediate and high Elo bands at one time control, then compare all copies on the same 1,500 boards. If the policies diverge further and the frozen probe consistently makes more than one extra error per hundred occupied squares, I would revise my conclusion.

5 What I would work on with Physical Reasoning

What excites me about probing a world model’s latent space is that it could show us what to teach it next. If a chess model loses track of pieces after exchanges, I’d use that finding to build training examples and test whether it learns to track the board more accurately and play stronger moves in new games.

I used AI to write code, analyze move choices, and prepare the diagrams.
